Prefer restraint and understatement in taste, avoiding showy or crude display.
Don't talk too much or show off your knowledge, even in your own field.
Respect experts and their practical wisdom, such as taking care at the easy-looking final stage.
Commit fully to each attempt without counting on a second chance, like using a single arrow.
Practice an art openly among skilled people while still unskilled, rather than waiting until you are good.
entries.argued_against: those who hide until they master an art

entries.advice: Don't hope for a long life; going beyond about forty invites unseemly clinging.
entries.argued_against: clinging to old age and worldly attachments

entries.advice: Value old customs and traditions over modern ways.
Choose friends wisely, avoiding the proud, the healthy who never suffer, the deceitful and the greedy.
Give up worldly ties and obligations to pursue the Way of awakening.
Leave things a little unfinished, since completeness invites decline.
Treasure intimate conversation with a truly like-minded companion.
Avoid wishing for many descendants.
Educate children early and strictly, starting even before birth, and discipline them while young.
Avoid showing favoritism among your children.
entries.argued_against: parents who dote on one child

entries.advice: Keep learning throughout life; even starting late is better than never.
Gain real learning and skills, which no one can take from you in times of upheaval.
entries.argued_against: relying on family rank and wealth

entries.advice: Be capable in practical affairs instead of being a pampered, useless aristocrat.
entries.argued_against: elite sons who couldn't ride or manage tasks

entries.advice: Be frugal without being stingy.
Keep harmony among brothers and their wives.
Be cautious about remarriage, since stepparents often harm the children of the first marriage.
Be careful in speech and writing, and avoid mocking or offending others.
Be content with modest office and wealth instead of seeking high rank.
Choose companions carefully, since you absorb their influence as clothing absorbs scent.
Respect the awakened one's teachings and avoid needless killing of living creatures.
Use correct pronunciation and properly written characters.
Don't pour resources into pursuing immortality, though moderate care of health is fine.
Give him a simple burial without lavish ceremony.
Make sure your reputation matches reality instead of seeking empty fame.
Treat borrowed books with care and return them in good condition.
Women should handle household matters rather than outside affairs.
Observe proper customs, such as avoiding the personal names of elders and ancestors.
Act through non-action: accomplish things without forcing or striving.
Be like water: soft, yielding and content with low places, which overcomes the hard.
Return to simplicity, like uncarved wood, and embrace plainness.
Reduce your desires and selfishness.
entries.argued_against: craving for sensory pleasures and goods

entries.advice: Know contentment and know when to stop, so you avoid disgrace and danger.
Don't boast, show off or claim credit; those who put themselves forward fail.
Govern lightly, with few laws and prohibitions, keeping the people's lives simple.
Avoid war; weapons are ill-omened, and even a victory should be treated as a funeral.
Abandon conventional cleverness, morality and learning, and the people will benefit.
entries.argued_against: promoters of humaneness, rightness and learning

entries.advice: Cultivate stillness and return to the root.
Treasure compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first.
entries.argued_against: courage without compassion, and pushing to the front

entries.advice: Deal with difficult things while they are easy and large things while they are small.
Know yourself and master yourself, which matters more than knowing and mastering others.
Speak little; those who know do not talk much.
Don't hoard wealth or honors; filling a hall with gold invites loss.
When your work is done, step back.
To lead the people, place yourself below and behind them.
Don't exalt the talented or prize rare goods, so people don't compete or steal.
Repay resentment with virtue.
Recognize the usefulness of emptiness, as in the hollow of a bowl or a room.
Prefer a small state with few people, content with simple lives and uninterested in travel.
Know your enemy and yourself, and you need not fear the outcome of battles.
entries.argued_against: commanders ignorant of themselves or the enemy

entries.advice: Aim to subdue the enemy without fighting; that is the highest skill.
Attack the enemy's strategy first, then alliances, then armies, and besiege walled cities only as a last resort.
Base warfare on deception: appear weak when strong, far when near.
Before war, carefully calculate and compare both sides on factors such as the moral cause, weather, terrain, command and discipline.
Avoid long campaigns; prolonged war exhausts the state.
Feed your army from the enemy's supplies to save your own resources.
Avoid the enemy's strengths and strike where they are weak or unprepared.
First make yourself invincible, then wait for the enemy to become vulnerable.
Combine direct and surprise forces in endlessly varied ways.
Stay formless and adapt to the enemy as water adapts to the ground.
Study the terrain carefully and use it to your advantage.
Use spies generously, since foreknowledge comes from people, not spirits or omens.
entries.argued_against: seeking knowledge from divination or spirits; stinginess with spies

entries.advice: Rulers should not interfere with a capable general in the field.
Care for soldiers like your children, but keep firm discipline.
Never go to war out of anger or resentment; act only when it is to your advantage.
entries.argued_against: rulers and generals who fight in rage

entries.advice: Leave a surrounded enemy a way out, and don't press a desperate foe.
Put your troops where they cannot retreat, so they will fight to the death.
Avoid a general's five dangerous faults: recklessness, cowardice, quick temper, touchy honor and excessive concern for the people.
Treat captured soldiers well and use them to strengthen yourself.
Use fire attacks only under the right weather and conditions.
Make your bright virtue shine, renew the people, and rest in the highest good.
entries.applies_to: those pursuing great learning, especially rulers

entries.advice: Follow the sequence: investigate things, extend knowledge, make intentions sincere, correct the mind, cultivate yourself, then order family and state.
entries.argued_against: trying to govern before cultivating oneself
entries.applies_to: those who would bring peace to the world

entries.advice: Treat self-cultivation as the root for everyone, from ruler to commoner.
entries.argued_against: neglecting the root while tending the branches

entries.advice: Know what comes first and what comes later, root and branch.
Know where to rest, so you can become settled, calm and able to deliberate.
Make your intentions sincere and don't deceive yourself; love good as you love beauty.
entries.argued_against: the petty person who hides evil and displays good

entries.advice: Be watchful over yourself when alone.
entries.argued_against: those who behave badly in private

entries.advice: Keep your mind from being thrown off balance by anger, fear, fondness or anxiety.
Notice how love and dislike bias your judgments of people.
entries.argued_against: partiality toward those we love or hate

entries.advice: Don't treat others as you dislike being treated by those above, below or beside you.
Rulers should value virtue over wealth; hoarding wealth scatters the people.
Love what the people love and hate what they hate.
Promote worthy people quickly and remove the bad decisively.
Let many produce and few consume, producing quickly and spending slowly.
Take rightness, not profit, as the state's true benefit.
Renew yourself daily, every day.
Hold to the mean, avoiding both excess and deficiency.
entries.argued_against: the petty person who acts without restraint

entries.advice: Be watchful and cautious even when alone and unseen.
Let your emotions arise in due measure so they stay balanced and harmonious.
Pursue sincerity, the way of heaven and the basis for fulfilling yourself and others.
Study broadly, ask carefully, reflect closely, distinguish clearly, and practice earnestly.
If others succeed with one effort, make a hundred; persistence overcomes dullness and weakness.
Act appropriately to your present position, rich or poor, without wanting what lies beyond it.
entries.argued_against: those who chase luck and resent heaven

entries.advice: When you fail, look for the cause in yourself, as an archer does when he misses.
Begin the Way with what is near, in the family and between husband and wife.
entries.argued_against: seeking the Way in remote places

entries.advice: Fulfill the five basic relationships through wisdom, humaneness and courage.
Don't seek strange or extraordinary deeds to win fame.
entries.argued_against: those who pursue the obscure and marvelous

entries.advice: Make your words match your deeds.
Do for others what you would want done for yourself, in each relationship.
Honor your parents and ancestors by carrying on their aims and keeping the ancestral rites.
Prepare in advance for every undertaking, since preparation brings success.
Rulers should follow nine standards, including cultivating themselves, honoring worthies and caring for the people.
Love learning to approach wisdom, practice hard to approach humaneness, and know shame to approach courage.
Recognize that human nature is bad, so goodness has to be produced by deliberate effort.
entries.argued_against: a rival thinker who held that human nature is good

entries.advice: Never stop learning; keep reshaping yourself as wood is straightened or metal sharpened.
Follow the rituals and standards of rightness made by the sages to order your desires.
Find a good teacher and follow him closely.
Build up small steps persistently; great results come from accumulation.
Choose your surroundings and companions carefully, since they shape your character.
Keep the mind empty, unified and still, so that partial views don't cloud it.
entries.argued_against: thinkers obsessed by one side of the truth

entries.advice: Don't fear strange natural events; heaven follows constant patterns, and human effort decides success.
Don't judge people by their physical appearance.
Use proper names consistently to keep order and prevent confusion.
Value proper music, which shapes emotions and brings harmony.
Keep the mourning and burial rites to honor the dead and express grief properly.
Satisfy desires within ritual limits rather than trying to eliminate them.
entries.argued_against: those who teach abolishing or reducing desires

entries.advice: Rulers should promote officials by virtue and ability, not birth.
Remember the ruler is the boat and the people the water that can carry or capsize it.
Treat those who rightly criticize you as teachers and flatterers as enemies.
Examine yourself daily.
Win wars by winning people's support through humane government, not by tricks.
Reject clever sophistry and arguments that don't serve real order.
See your own original nature, which is inherently awakened; awakening comes from realizing it, not from outside.
entries.argued_against: seeking awakening outside one's own mind

entries.advice: Awakening can happen suddenly, not only by gradual stages.
Practice no-thought: let thoughts come and go without attaching to them.
Understand meditation and wisdom as one, like a lamp and its light.
entries.argued_against: those who separate them in sequence

entries.advice: Real seated meditation means an unmoved mind, not sitting motionless and staring at the mind.
entries.argued_against: teachers of rigid sitting and contemplating purity

entries.advice: Don't expect building temples or giving alms to earn spiritual merit; merit lies in your own nature.
entries.argued_against: a ruler who expected merit from donations

entries.advice: Purify your own mind, since the pure land is found there, not far to the west.
entries.argued_against: seeking rebirth elsewhere instead of purifying the mind

entries.advice: You can practice at home as a layperson; you need not enter a monastery.
entries.argued_against: the view that only monks can practice

entries.advice: Take refuge in the awakened one, the teaching and the community within your own nature.
entries.argued_against: taking refuge only in external objects

entries.advice: Repent formlessly by vowing never again to commit past errors in thought.
Don't look at other people's faults; attend to your own.
Don't just recite scriptures; understand their meaning and turn them, rather than letting them turn you.
entries.argued_against: a monk proud of reciting a scripture many times

entries.advice: Understand that fundamentally there is nothing to wipe clean, since original nature is never defiled.
entries.argued_against: the verse calling for constant polishing of the mind

entries.advice: Recognize that wisdom is equally present in everyone, whatever their origin or education.
entries.argued_against: contempt for an unlettered southern rustic

entries.advice: Don't cling to emptiness by sitting with an empty mind, nor to forms.
When teaching, use paired opposites so the listener drops both extremes and reaches the middle.
After the teacher's death, don't weep or wear mourning, which goes against the teaching.
Treat devotion to your parents as the root of all virtue and the starting point of all moral teaching.
entries.applies_to: everyone, from the ruler to the common people

entries.advice: Do not injure or damage your body, hair, or skin, since you received them from your parents.
entries.applies_to: children toward their parents; the beginning of filial conduct

entries.advice: Establish yourself, walk the right way, and make a good name for later generations so that your parents are honored.
Begin filial devotion by serving your parents, continue it by serving the ruler, and complete it by establishing your own character.
entries.applies_to: everyone over the course of life

entries.advice: As a supreme ruler, love and respect your own parents and never show contempt toward others' parents, so the people follow your example.
As a lord in high position, avoid arrogance and be careful and moderate in spending so you keep your wealth and rank without danger.
entries.argued_against: arrogance and extravagance of the powerful

entries.advice: As a high official, wear only proper clothing, speak only approved words, and act only according to the conduct of the ancient sage-kings.
entries.argued_against: conduct that departs from the ancient standards

entries.advice: Serve your ruler with the same reverence and your elders with the same love you show your father, being loyal and deferential.
Follow the seasons, use the land well, behave carefully, and spend frugally in order to support your parents.
At home show utmost reverence to parents; feed them gladly, worry when they are ill, grieve at their death, and sacrifice solemnly.
entries.applies_to: children serving their parents throughout life and after death

entries.advice: Avoid arrogance when in high position, insubordination when in low position, and quarrelling among your equals.
entries.argued_against: those who are arrogant, rebellious, or contentious, even if they feed their parents well

entries.advice: Regard failing in filial duty as the greatest of all crimes; never coerce your ruler, reject the sages, or deny filial devotion.
entries.argued_against: those who coerce rulers, disparage sages, and dismiss filial piety

entries.advice: When your father or ruler is about to do wrong, remonstrate with them rather than simply obeying.
entries.argued_against: the view that obeying every command of one's father is filial
entries.applies_to: sons, ministers, and friends facing wrongdoing by their superiors

entries.advice: As a ruler, govern through filial devotion and do not neglect even the lowliest subjects, widows, or widowers.
Teach people love through filial piety, respect through deference to elders, and reform customs through ritual and music.
entries.argued_against: governing by harshness rather than example
entries.applies_to: rulers and teachers of the people

entries.advice: In mourning a parent, weep without prolonged wailing, keep rites without display, speak plainly, avoid fine food and music, and not harm your health.
entries.argued_against: mourning so excessive that it destroys one's life
entries.applies_to: children mourning parents, for three years

entries.advice: Offer seasonal sacrifices to your ancestors in the ancestral temple with reverence and remember them.
In serving a ruler, think of being fully loyal when in office and of correcting his faults when away, supporting his good and checking his bad.
Do not love or respect others while failing to love and respect your own parents; that is a perversion of virtue.
entries.argued_against: those who neglect their own parents yet show love to others

entries.advice: Transfer the order of a well-run household into your public office, and your respect for elders into obedience to superiors.
Recognize that the mind comes before all actions; act and speak with a pure mind, and happiness follows you like a shadow.
entries.argued_against: acting and speaking from a corrupted mind

entries.advice: Let go of grudges, because hatred is never ended by hatred, only by non-hatred.
entries.argued_against: those who brood over insults and injuries

entries.advice: Be vigilant and heedful at all times; heedlessness is the path to death.
Guard, tame, and straighten your restless, wavering mind, since a well-trained mind brings happiness.
Do not kill or cause killing; all beings fear violence, so compare others with yourself.
Avoid all evil, do good, and purify your mind.
Keep company with the wise and good; if you find no worthy companion, walk alone rather than with fools.
Conquer yourself, which is greater than conquering thousands of people in battle.
entries.argued_against: those who glory in conquering others

entries.advice: Live by the teaching rather than merely reciting many scriptures without practicing them.
entries.argued_against: learned people who recite much but do not act

entries.advice: Look at your own faults and what you have and have not done, not at others' faults.
entries.argued_against: those who seek out others' faults

entries.advice: Speak no harsh words to anyone, because angry speech brings pain back upon you.
Overcome anger by calmness, evil by good, stinginess by giving, and lies by truth.
Do not dismiss small wrongs or small good deeds; like drops filling a jar, they accumulate.
entries.argued_against: those who think a little evil will not matter

entries.advice: Root out craving entirely, since it grows like a creeper and brings endless sorrow.
Do not cling to what is dear or pleasant, because grief and fear arise from attachment.
Reflect that the body is frail, impermanent, and headed for old age and death, like foam or a mirage.
entries.argued_against: those who are complacent about the body and life

entries.advice: Value health, contentment, and trust as the greatest gains and wealth.
Judge a person holy by conduct and purity, not by birth, family, or hairstyle.
entries.argued_against: the view that holiness comes from birth or outward marks

entries.advice: Do not rely on outward austerities like nakedness, matted hair, fasting, or lying in dust to purify you.
entries.argued_against: ascetics who trust in external practices

entries.advice: Make the effort yourself and be your own refuge; teachers only point out the way.
entries.argued_against: relying on others for one's purification

entries.advice: Abstain from killing, stealing, lying, going to others' spouses, and drinking intoxicants.
entries.argued_against: those who do such things and dig up their own roots

entries.advice: Stay unshaken by praise and blame, like a solid rock unmoved by wind.
Live happily without hatred among the hateful and without possessiveness among the greedy.
Cultivate both meditation and wisdom, since neither arises fully without the other.
Practice restraint of body, speech, and mind, and of the senses.
Pursue virtue without ceasing, since it is the source of both happiness and lasting reputation.
Honor the household life as the best way to live, supporting family, ascetics, the poor, ancestors, and guests.
entries.argued_against: the view that only renunciation is virtuous

entries.advice: Welcome guests with a cheerful face and feed them before eating yourself.
entries.argued_against: those who hoard food and neglect guests

entries.advice: Speak kindly and sweetly rather than harshly, as choosing harsh words over sweet ones is like eating unripe fruit when ripe is available.
Never forget a kindness done to you, however small; ingratitude is the one wrong that cannot be redeemed.
Do not kill any living being and abstain from eating meat.
entries.argued_against: those who kill or eat flesh

entries.advice: Do not speak ill of others behind their backs.
Avoid envy and do not covet the property of others.
Bear insults and injuries patiently, as the earth bears those who dig into it.
Be truthful; speak what harms no one, though a falsehood that brings faultless good counts as truth.
Never desire another person's wife.
Learn thoroughly what is worth learning, and then live according to it.
entries.argued_against: the unlearned and those who learn without practicing

entries.advice: Listen to the learned and wise, since hearing good counsel is a great treasure.
As a ruler, govern justly, protect your subjects, be easy to approach, and avoid harsh words and cruel punishments.
Test people carefully before making them friends, and avoid false friends who only seem friendly.
Avoid drunkenness, gambling, and prostitutes.
entries.argued_against: drinkers, gamblers, those who keep harlots

entries.advice: Deliberate before acting, then persevere with effort; diligent effort can overcome even fate.
entries.argued_against: those who blame fate and give up

entries.advice: Avoid laziness, procrastination, forgetfulness, and excessive sleep.
Give to the poor who cannot repay you; that is true charity.
Earn wealth by honest means, since rightly acquired wealth makes virtue and happiness possible.
Cherish love for others; a body without love is merely bones covered with skin.
Do good even to those who harm you, so that they are shamed.
Avoid anger, which destroys oneself and one's joy.
Practice humility and self-control, because self-restraint leads to honor.
Cherish faithful, devoted love between partners, including its quarrels and reconciliations.
Realize that your innermost self is identical with the ultimate reality underlying everything.
entries.argued_against: seeing oneself as separate from the ultimate

entries.advice: Seek knowledge of the self rather than relying on rituals, which yield only temporary rewards.
entries.argued_against: ritualists who think sacrifices lead to the highest good

entries.advice: Approach a qualified teacher humbly, with fuel in hand, to learn about the self.
Choose the good over the merely pleasant, as the wise do.
Control your senses as a charioteer controls horses, with the intellect as driver and the mind as reins.
Enjoy the world through renunciation and do not covet anyone's wealth.
Keep doing your works while hoping to live a hundred years; action done thus does not bind you.
Practice self-restraint, giving, and compassion.
entries.applies_to: the divine beings, humans, and demons respectively, and so everyone

entries.advice: Speak the truth, do your duty, keep up study, and honor mother, father, teacher, and guest as divine.
Give with faith, generosity, modesty, awe, and understanding, never without faith.
Meditate on the sacred syllable as a means to reach the ultimate.
Recognize that your desire shapes your will, your will your deeds, and your deeds your destiny.
Do not expect wealth to bring immortality; seek knowledge of the self instead.
entries.argued_against: those who seek fulfillment in wealth

entries.advice: Understand that spouse, children, and wealth are dear for the sake of the self, so seek to know the self.
See all beings in the self and the self in all beings, and you will hate no one.
Reject worldly pleasures, long life, and riches when offered, in favor of knowledge of what lies beyond death.
Do not pursue ignorance alone or knowledge alone; those who do enter darkness.
Honor food, never despise it, and produce plenty of it.
Value truth, which alone triumphs, not falsehood.
Practice austerity, chastity, and faith as means to know the self.
Do not expect to grasp the self by mere learning, intellect, or much study; seek it with a calm, restrained mind.
Give up desires of the heart, since one freed from desire attains the ultimate.
Seek the company of good people, because it removes dullness, inspires truthful speech, and increases honor.
Value learning as your true wealth and ornament; it cannot be stolen and grows when shared.
entries.argued_against: those without learning, who are like beasts

entries.advice: Do not waste effort trying to persuade an obstinate fool; it is harder than taming wild beasts.
Persist steadily in good undertakings and never swerve from the just path, whether praised or blamed, rich or poor.
entries.argued_against: those who give up at obstacles

entries.advice: Value refined, cultured speech as the only lasting ornament, more than bracelets or garlands.
Help others without being asked and without seeking reward, as noble people do.
entries.argued_against: those who harm others for no gain

entries.advice: Give your wealth away or enjoy it, since wealth neither given nor enjoyed will simply be lost.
Avoid wicked people even if they are learned, as one avoids a serpent though it wears a jewel.
Prize honor and self-respect over life itself and comfort.
entries.argued_against: those who trade honor for gain

entries.advice: Cultivate patience and forbearance, which serve as armor.
Recognize that craving never grows old even as you age, and give it up.
Be content with little; the content and the rich are equal, and the discontented is truly poor.
Avoid humiliating service and flattery of the rich and of kings.
Recognize that everything in life is shadowed by fear, and only renunciation is free of fear.
Reflect that youth, beauty, wealth, and life are fleeting and that time devours everything.
Seek a simple life in the forest, living on alms and meditating on the divine.
Appreciate erotic love and women's charms, but know they can bind and delude a person.
entries.applies_to: lovers and those weighing pleasure against renunciation

entries.advice: Acknowledge the power of fate while still acting rightly.
Avoid pride in your own little learning; knowledge should humble you.
Cultivate boundless loving-kindness toward all beings, as a mother protects her only child.
entries.applies_to: those skilled in the good who seek peace

entries.advice: Wander alone like a rhinoceros horn rather than tie yourself to companions, unless you find a wise one.
Judge people as noble or outcast by their deeds, not their birth.
entries.argued_against: the view that birth determines worth

entries.advice: Avoid the causes of downfall: laziness, drunkenness, gambling, womanizing, neglecting aged parents, and pride of birth.
Support parents, cherish spouse and children, give, avoid evil, be respectful, humble, grateful, and patient.
Avoid sensual desires, which bring pain like a wound or a dart.
Do not cling to views or argue that your view is best; avoid disputes.
Regard nothing as yours, freeing yourself from possessiveness.
Speak what is well said, pleasant, true, and in accord with the teaching.
Do not kill, steal, lie, drink intoxicants, or engage in sexual misconduct.
Understand that real defilement is evil conduct, not eating certain foods or skipping rituals.
entries.argued_against: those who see purity in diet, bathing, or sacrifice

entries.advice: Accept that death comes to all; pull out the arrow of grief, since lamenting does not help.
Strive energetically and resist the forces of temptation, preferring death in battle to defeated life.
Value a true friend who does not seek your faults and stays loyal, not a flatterer.
Be capable, upright, easy to speak to, gentle, humble, content, and lightly burdened.
Cross the flood of suffering through faith, heedfulness, energy, and wisdom.
Be a renunciant in practice, not merely in appearance or words.
Avoid anger, conceit, deceit, and greed.
Give generously to those who are worthy, with a pure mind.
Do your duty without attachment to its results.
entries.argued_against: acting for the sake of rewards

entries.advice: Perform your own duty, even imperfectly, rather than another's duty well.
Stay even-minded in pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat.
Do not grieve over death, since the true self is eternal and is never killed.
entries.applies_to: the warrior facing battle, and everyone

entries.advice: Do not abandon action out of weakness or confusion; action is unavoidable and better than inaction.
Offer all your actions to the divine as a sacrifice.
Control your senses, withdrawing them from objects as a tortoise withdraws its limbs.
Overcome desire, anger, and greed, the three gates of ruin.
Meditate in a clean, quiet place with a steady posture and a focused, calm mind.
Be moderate in eating, sleeping, recreation, and work.
entries.argued_against: those who eat or sleep too much or too little

entries.advice: Worship the divine with loving devotion; even a leaf, flower, fruit, or water offered with love is accepted.
Learn wisdom from the wise by humble inquiry and service.
See the divine in all beings and treat friend and foe alike.
Cultivate fearlessness, purity, charity, self-control, nonviolence, truthfulness, and freedom from anger.
Prefer the pure kinds of food, sacrifice, austerity, and charity over the passionate and dull kinds.
Give to a worthy recipient at the proper time and place, expecting nothing in return.
entries.argued_against: giving for gain or with contempt

entries.advice: Do not be captivated by flowery scriptural promises of heavenly rewards.
Take refuge in the divine alone, surrendering all other duties.
Keep the divine in mind at all times, including at the moment of death.
Avoid doubt and faithlessness, as the doubter finds happiness neither here nor hereafter.
Act for the welfare of the world and set an example, as others follow the great.
Speak words that are truthful, pleasant, beneficial, and not upsetting.
Hate no being; be friendly, compassionate, free of ego, and forgiving.
Aim to still the fluctuations of the mind so the seer rests in its true nature.
Combine steady practice with nonattachment to quiet the mind.
Practice for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion to make it firmly grounded.
Devote yourself to the supreme lord, a special self untouched by affliction.
Repeat the sacred syllable while contemplating its meaning.
Cultivate friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous, and indifference toward the wicked.
Observe nonviolence, truthfulness, non-stealing, sexual restraint, and non-possessiveness.
entries.applies_to: everyone, universally regardless of class, place, time, or circumstance

entries.advice: Practice purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the lord.
When troubled by harmful thoughts, cultivate their opposites.
Take a posture that is steady and comfortable.
Regulate your breath.
Withdraw your senses from their objects.
Practice concentration, meditation, and absorption on a single object.
Avoid future suffering by removing its cause, the confusion of seer with seen.
Weaken ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life through disciplined practice.
Develop discriminating insight between pure awareness and the world of nature.
Do not take pride in or be seduced by special powers or the flattery of celestial beings.
Overcome obstacles like illness, doubt, laziness, and carelessness by focusing on one principle.
Practice with faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and insight.
Practice nonattachment even toward the highest discriminative knowledge to reach liberation.
Value this human life as rare and precious, and use it for awakening before it is lost.
Resolve to attain awakening for the benefit of all beings.
Confess your past wrongs with regret and resolve not to repeat them.
Dedicate all your merit to relieving the suffering of all beings.
Guard your mind with mindfulness and introspection, since controlling the mind controls all dangers.
When the urge to speak or act from anger or pride arises, stay still like a log.
Practice patience, since no evil equals hatred and anger destroys accumulated good.
Value enemies as teachers who give you the chance to practice patience.
Do not be angry at those who harm you; they are driven by afflictions, like a stick wielded by a hand.
Cultivate joyful enthusiasm for virtue and overcome laziness and discouragement.
Withdraw to solitude to meditate, turning away from worldly attachments and foolish company.
Reflect on the body's impurity to weaken lust.
Treat others as equal to yourself and exchange yourself for others, since wanting only your own happiness causes all suffering.
Give generously, even your body, when the time is right.
Understand that the self and phenomena lack inherent existence.
Rejoice in others' good fortune rather than envying them.
Train by accepting small hardships first so that greater ones become bearable.
Behave with restraint: speak gently, move quietly, and keep your gaze lowered.
Serve all beings, since this pleases the awakened ones.
Remember that death may come at any time, and practice urgently.
As a ruler, master your senses by giving up lust, anger, greed, conceit, arrogance, and excessive joy.
As a ruler, regard your subjects' welfare and happiness as your own.
entries.argued_against: rulers who seek only personal pleasure

entries.advice: As a ruler, be energetic and keep a strict daily schedule for administration, councils, and rest.
Study philosophy, sacred lore, economics, and government, and keep company with learned elders.
Avoid hunting, gambling, women, and drink, the vices arising from desire.
Appoint ministers only after secretly testing their honesty and loyalty.
Use a network of spies to monitor officials, subjects, and foreign powers.
Treat neighboring states as natural enemies and those beyond them as natural allies.
Choose peace, war, waiting, marching, alliance, or a mixed policy depending on your relative strength.
Punish justly: too severe punishment terrifies, too mild invites contempt.
Keep the treasury full, since all undertakings depend on finances.
Guard against officials embezzling funds through careful supervision and audits.
Protect and support the helpless: orphans, the elderly, the sick, and widows.
Uphold the duties of each social class and stage of life.
Regard material prosperity as the foundation of virtue and pleasure.
entries.argued_against: those who rank virtue or pleasure higher

entries.advice: Guard yourself against plots by princes, queens, and courtiers.
Prefer conciliation, then gifts, then sowing dissension, and use force only last.
Eliminate traitors and dangerous enemies by secret means where necessary.
After conquest, win over the people by respecting their customs and replacing the defeated king's vices with virtues.
Develop agriculture, mining, irrigation, trade, and settlement of new land.
Do not rely too much on the stars; opportunity slips from the fool who keeps consulting them.
Follow the path of virtue, concentration, and understanding to reach purification.
Keep the monastic code, restrain the senses, earn a pure livelihood, and use requisites with reflection.
Avoid wrong livelihood such as scheming, flattery, hinting, and pressuring for gifts.
Eat food only to sustain the body for practice, not for enjoyment or beautification.
Take up ascetic practices suited to your temperament to support contentment and fewness of wishes.
Cut off impediments such as attachment to dwelling, family, gain, followers, and travel.
Find a good spiritual friend and teacher to give you a meditation subject.
Choose a meditation subject suited to your temperament, such as foulness for the lustful and loving-kindness for the hateful.
Live in a suitable dwelling and avoid monasteries with faults such as noise or crowds.
Develop loving-kindness first toward yourself, then a dear person, a neutral person, and finally an enemy.
When resentment toward an enemy arises, reflect on the teaching, their good qualities, and that anger harms yourself.
Recollect death regularly.
Contemplate the thirty-two parts of the body.
Practice mindfulness of breathing.
Balance faith with wisdom and energy with concentration.
Contemplate impermanence, suffering, and non-self in all formations.
Do not cling to experiences like light or rapture during insight; they are imperfections, not the path.
Understand dependent origination to overcome doubt about past, present, and future.
Reflect on the repulsiveness of food to reduce greed for flavors.
Pursue virtue, wealth, and pleasure in balance, without letting one harm the others.
entries.argued_against: those who pursue only one aim
entries.applies_to: everyone, varying by stage of life

entries.advice: Study the science of love and the sixty-four arts.
entries.argued_against: those who say love needs no study since animals mate naturally

entries.advice: Rely on effort and means rather than fate.
After education, set up a refined household and follow a routine of grooming, bathing, and cultured leisure.
Marry a woman of equal class and good family, and avoid unsuitable brides.
Win a new bride's trust gradually and gently rather than forcing intimacy.
As a wife, manage the household and finances wisely and respect your husband's family.
Attend to your partner's pleasure and satisfaction, not only your own.
Avoid relations with other men's wives except in extreme circumstances.
Avoid certain women, such as relatives, the sick, and wives of friends or of rulers.
Respect regional customs and your partner's preferences rather than using every technique.
Use the teaching wisely and with self-control, not to fuel lust.
entries.argued_against: those who indulge passion without restraint

entries.advice: As a courtesan, choose lovers carefully, manage them for gain, and end liaisons when they are no longer profitable.
Use go-betweens and careful courtship to win a desired partner.
Match partners according to their size, temperament, and stamina.
Value human birth, longing for liberation, and a great teacher's guidance as rare gifts.
Discriminate between the real and the unreal, the self and the not-self.
Cultivate dispassion, calm, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, faith, concentration, and intense longing for liberation.
Approach a wise teacher humbly, serve them, and ask your questions.
Seek liberation through realizing the self's identity with the ultimate, not through rituals or works.
Do not mistake scholarship and scriptural learning for realization.
Recognize the body, life-force, mind, intellect, and bliss sheaths as not the self.
Give up identifying yourself with the body.
entries.argued_against: the notion that one is the body

entries.advice: Renounce sense objects, which destroy creatures attached to even one sense, like the moth or deer.
Meditate constantly on your identity with the ultimate.
Eliminate latent tendencies and the ego.
Never be careless about contemplation; carelessness is death.
Make your own effort; others can pay debts for you, but no one else can free you.
Practice hearing the teaching, reflecting on it, and meditating on it deeply.
See the world as superimposed on the self, like a snake mistaken for a rope.
Once liberated, live free, unaffected by praise or blame.
Focus only on what is within your control: your judgments, choices, and actions.
Remember that it is your opinion about things, not the things themselves, that disturbs you.
Expect to meet meddling, ungrateful, arrogant people each day, and do not be angry, since they act from ignorance.
Live in accordance with nature and reason, as a part of the rational whole.
Work for the common good, as humans are made for cooperation like feet, hands, and eyelids.
Remember death often and live each day as if it were your last.
entries.argued_against: acting as if you had endless time

entries.advice: Accept whatever happens as part of the order of the universe.
Do not crave posthumous fame; those who remember you will soon die too.
Get up in the morning to do the work of a human being rather than staying in warm blankets.
Retreat into your own mind for peace rather than seeking retreats in the country or seashore.
The best revenge is not to be like the wrongdoer.
Learn from others' virtues, as shown by gratitude to family and teachers in the first part.
entries.applies_to: the writer reflecting on his upbringing

entries.advice: Analyze pleasures and impressive things into their components to strip them of false glamour.
Do not waste time guessing what others think of you or worrying about others' affairs.
Stop arguing about what a good person is; be one.
Do each task with full attention, seriousness, and justice, as if it were your last.
Be willing to be corrected and change your mind when shown wrong.
Do not be made into a tyrant by power; stay simple, good, and sincere.
Endure pain by recognizing that it is either bearable or will end.
Reflect on the vastness of time and smallness of human life to keep perspective.
Do good without expecting thanks, like a vine bearing grapes.
Avoid anger; gentleness is more manly and strong.
Turn away from worldly vanities such as riches, honors, and pleasures, and seek lasting things instead.
entries.argued_against: those who chase wealth, honor, and comfort in this passing world
entries.applies_to: all who wish to follow the savior

entries.advice: Think humbly of yourself and value being unknown and little regarded.
entries.argued_against: proud people who want to be esteemed and think themselves better than others

entries.advice: Value a holy life and a clear conscience over learning, clever argument, and knowledge.
entries.argued_against: learned people who dispute subtle questions but neglect virtue

entries.advice: Read sacred books for truth and spiritual profit, humbly and simply, not for eloquence or to look learned.
entries.argued_against: reading for style, curiosity, or reputation
entries.applies_to: readers of scripture and devout books

entries.advice: Love solitude and silence, avoid needless talk and company, and stay in your cell.
entries.argued_against: those who seek news, gossip, and constant company

entries.advice: Don't pry into other people's affairs or what others say and do; attend to your own soul.
Judge yourself rather than others, and avoid rash judgments about their actions.
entries.argued_against: people who condemn others while excusing themselves

entries.advice: Bear patiently with other people's faults and weaknesses, since others must bear with yours.
entries.argued_against: those who want others perfect while not correcting themselves
entries.applies_to: people living in community with others

entries.advice: Resist temptation at its first beginning, before it grows strong; accept temptations as tests that humble and teach you.
entries.argued_against: those who give in a little and delay resistance
entries.applies_to: everyone, since no one in this life is free from temptation

entries.advice: Keep death in mind daily and live each day as if you might die before evening.
entries.argued_against: those who expect long life and put off amendment

entries.advice: Don't put off repentance and improvement; use the present time well.
entries.argued_against: those who trust in future time or in others to pray for them after death

entries.advice: Obey your superior willingly and give up your own opinion rather than insisting on your way.
entries.argued_against: those who obey grudgingly or hold to their own judgment
entries.applies_to: those living under a superior, especially members of religious communities

entries.advice: Take up your cross and accept suffering and hardship willingly, following the savior.
entries.argued_against: those who love the savior's consolations but flee his sufferings

entries.advice: Put your trust in the deity rather than in people, who are changeable and unreliable.
entries.argued_against: relying on friends, human favor, or oneself

entries.advice: Love the savior above everything and seek close inward friendship with him.
entries.argued_against: loving creatures or oneself for their own sake

entries.advice: Give up self-will and self-love, mastering your passions to gain inner peace.
entries.argued_against: those ruled by their own desires and inclinations

entries.advice: Don't seek human praise or worry about people's opinions; care only how the deity sees you.
entries.argued_against: those who live for others' approval

entries.advice: Examine your conscience daily, renew your resolutions each morning, and review your conduct each evening.
entries.argued_against: careless, lukewarm religious people who neglect self-examination

entries.advice: Stay steady when spiritual comfort is withdrawn, and don't depend on consolations or feelings of devotion.
entries.argued_against: those who serve the deity only for consolation
entries.applies_to: people in times of spiritual dryness

entries.advice: Receive the sacrament of the altar often, with reverence, humility, and careful preparation.
entries.argued_against: those who approach it carelessly or neglect it through sloth
entries.applies_to: believers, and priests who celebrate it

entries.advice: Avoid familiarity with women and with young people and strangers; don't seek the company of the great.
entries.argued_against: seeking intimacy with the powerful or with many people

entries.advice: Act with a pure, simple intention, doing everything for the deity rather than for personal gain.
entries.argued_against: seeking one's own advantage in good works

entries.advice: Be fervent and diligent in spiritual practice and keep up good habits; don't grow lukewarm.
entries.argued_against: lax and negligent religious who fall from their first fervor

entries.advice: Guard your time as your only true possession; stop letting it be taken or wasted.
entries.argued_against: people who give away their time freely while guarding money

entries.advice: Read a few chosen authors deeply instead of skipping restlessly through many books.
Take one useful thought from your reading each day to digest, even from an opposing school.
Practice poverty now and then by living for a few days on plain food and rough clothing.
entries.argued_against: those who fear poverty without ever testing it
entries.applies_to: people who are comfortable and prosperous

entries.advice: Avoid crowds and public spectacles, which pass on vices; keep company with people who improve you.
entries.applies_to: especially those still weak in character

entries.advice: Practice for death daily and stop fearing it; it is natural and no evil.
entries.argued_against: those who fear death and cling to life

entries.advice: Judge carefully before making a friend; once you accept someone, trust them fully.
entries.argued_against: those who trust before judging or judge after trusting

entries.advice: Make philosophy a matter of action, not words: live by what you say.
entries.argued_against: those who treat philosophy as clever talk or display

entries.advice: Don't make a show of philosophy with odd dress, unkempt hair, or eccentric habits; live plainly but normally.
Limit your desires to natural needs; nature asks little, and luxury breeds endless wants.
Be able to own wealth without depending on it, so losing it would not disturb you.
Treat slaves humanely, talk and eat with them, and remember they share your nature.
Don't expect travel to cure your unease; you carry your troubled mind with you wherever you go.
entries.argued_against: restless people who keep changing places

entries.advice: Imagine an admired good person watching you, and act as if they were present.
Don't torment yourself with imagined future troubles; we suffer more in fear than in reality.
Consider virtue, guided by reason, the only true good; ignore what fortune gives and takes.
Accept fate willingly and follow it rather than being dragged along by it.
entries.argued_against: those who complain against events and the deity

entries.advice: Remember that you can leave life if it becomes unbearable, so no one is truly trapped.
entries.argued_against: those who think they must endure anything to stay alive
entries.applies_to: people facing extreme suffering or tyranny

entries.advice: Withdraw from busy public affairs and ambition into leisure devoted to philosophy.
entries.argued_against: those consumed by office and business

entries.advice: Don't waste time on logical quibbles and word-puzzles; study what makes you better.
entries.argued_against: philosophers who indulge in trivial dialectic

entries.advice: Exercise the body briefly and moderately, and give most of your effort to the mind.
entries.argued_against: those obsessed with athletics and building muscle

entries.advice: Grieve for those who die in moderation, and remember them gladly instead of mourning without end.
Examine yourself and your faults honestly, as an accuser and judge of yourself.
entries.argued_against: those blind to their own vices

entries.advice: Value old age, which can be pleasant if used well, and live each day as complete.
entries.argued_against: those who dread or waste old age

entries.advice: Obey the abbot promptly, willingly, and without delay or grumbling, as if obeying the deity.
entries.argued_against: those who obey slowly, halfheartedly, or with complaint

entries.advice: Keep silence and speak rarely, gently, and seriously; avoid gossip, coarse jokes, and loud laughter.
entries.argued_against: chatter, idle talk, and frivolous laughter
entries.applies_to: monks, especially at night and at meals

entries.advice: Climb the steps of humility: fear the deity, renounce self-will, accept hardship, confess faults, and think yourself lowest.
Pray the divine office at the fixed hours of day and night, and put nothing before it.
entries.argued_against: those who come late to or neglect the office

entries.advice: Divide each day between manual labor and sacred reading, because idleness is the soul's enemy.
entries.applies_to: monks, with schedules varying by season

entries.advice: Own nothing privately; receive what you need from the abbot and hold everything in common.
As abbot, teach more by example than by words, adapt to each person, and seek to be loved rather than feared.
Care for the sick above all, serving them as you would the savior, with baths and meat when needed.
entries.applies_to: the community and those assigned to the sick

entries.advice: Welcome every guest as the savior, especially the poor and pilgrims, with humility and care.
Eat and drink in moderation: two cooked dishes, a measured portion of wine, and no meat of four-footed animals.
entries.applies_to: monks; exceptions for the sick, weak, young, and heavy workers

entries.advice: During Lent add some extra self-denial in food, sleep, or talk, but only with the abbot's approval.
Correct faults step by step: private warnings first, then public rebuke, exclusion, and finally expulsion.
entries.applies_to: the abbot and seniors dealing with offenders

entries.advice: Avoid grumbling above all; do assigned tasks without murmuring.
Keep the order of rank by entry; juniors honor seniors and seniors love juniors.
entries.argued_against: rank based on age or worldly status alone

entries.advice: Test newcomers strictly over a long period, reading them the rule, before they promise stability, conversion, and obedience.
entries.applies_to: novices and those who receive them

entries.advice: On important matters the abbot should consult the whole community, even the youngest, then decide himself.
Treat all the monastery's tools and goods as carefully as sacred altar vessels.
entries.argued_against: careless or wasteful handling of property

entries.advice: Sleep clothed, in separate beds, in a lit dormitory, ready to rise for the night office.
Never defend or strike another monk on your own authority.
entries.argued_against: factions and taking punishment into one's own hands

entries.advice: Obey one another as well as the abbot, and practice good zeal: patience, mutual respect, and love.
entries.argued_against: bitter zeal that leads away from the deity

entries.advice: Practice crafts humbly; if proud of your skill, stop; sell products slightly below worldly prices.
Don't leave the monastery without permission, and don't tell others what you saw outside.
Love the deity and neighbor, don't repay evil with evil, and keep death daily before your eyes.
Treat this rule as a modest beginning, then go on to higher teaching for perfection.
Separate what is up to you (judgments, desires, aversions) from what is not (body, property, reputation, office).
entries.argued_against: those who treat external things as their own

entries.advice: Desire only, and avoid only, things within your control; for now hold back desire entirely.
entries.argued_against: those who want or fear external things

entries.advice: Remind yourself what loved things really are: a breakable jug, a mortal child or spouse.
entries.applies_to: everyone with possessions and loved ones

entries.advice: Recognize that your judgments about events disturb you, not the events themselves.
entries.argued_against: those who blame events or others for their distress

entries.advice: When you lose something, say you have given it back rather than lost it.
entries.applies_to: people facing loss, including death of family

entries.advice: Want things to happen as they actually happen, not as you wish.
Play well the role the playwright assigns you, whether short, long, poor, or official.
Blame neither others nor yourself for your troubles.
Accept looking foolish or ignorant about external matters if you want to progress.
Take what life offers politely, as at a banquet, without grabbing or waiting impatiently.
Keep silent mostly; avoid common talk about gladiators, horse races, food, and praising or blaming people.
Don't laugh much or loudly, avoid oaths, and avoid vulgar parties and obscene talk.
Go to public shows rarely; if you go, don't take sides or get excited.
Stay pure in sex before marriage as far as possible, without censuring those who don't.
When someone speaks ill of you, don't defend yourself; say they missed your other faults.
entries.applies_to: people who are insulted or criticized

entries.advice: Measure duties by relationships: honor a father, treat a brother as a brother, whatever their behavior.
entries.argued_against: those who ask whether others deserve their duty

entries.advice: Hold correct beliefs about the gods, that they rule well, and yield to events.
Consult diviners only about things not up to you, and don't let omens override duty.
Don't call yourself a philosopher or lecture about principles; act on them and practice austerity privately.
Think through what an undertaking requires and its consequences before committing to it.
entries.argued_against: those who rush in like children
entries.applies_to: anyone starting a project or career, including philosophy

entries.advice: Provide for the body only what it needs in food, drink, clothing, and housing; avoid luxury.
Take each matter by the bearable handle, e.g., a wronging brother is still your brother.
Keep death, exile, and other apparent terrors before your eyes daily to avoid base thoughts and greed.
Start with small losses, like spilled oil or stolen wine, treating them as the price of tranquility.
Stop postponing improvement; act now as if you were a grown adult in the contest.
Worship the deity, who is mind, with a pure mind.
Love your parents and honor your relatives, and overcome a parent's harshness with patience.
Stay watchful and sleep only as much as needed, not giving yourself to sleep.
Consider restraining your tongue the first virtue; speak little, especially at banquets.
Don't blame others for faults, since no one lives without fault; don't do what you criticize.
Give up harmful things even if you love them.
Don't argue with wordy people; speech is given to all, wisdom to few.
Avoid spreading rumors, and don't readily believe what you hear.
Don't fear death, which ends life's ills.
Beware of flatterers and smooth talkers; match pretense with pretense when someone deceives you with words.
Control your anger; don't get angry without serious cause, since anger blocks judgment.
Read books and remember what you read; keep learning.
Educate your children and teach them a trade.
Guard your property, spend carefully, and lend thoughtfully, watching to whom you give.
Be generous to good people and remember favors you receive.
Drink wine moderately, dine out rarely, and avoid dice and prostitutes.
Don't mock the unfortunate or laugh at anyone.
Yield to those greater than you and spare those lesser; avoid contending with the powerful.
Keep oaths and what is entrusted to you, and never lie.
Be content with what you have and live within modest means.
Don't put faith in dreams or omens.
Keep company with good people and don't give advice before being asked.
Fight for your country and obey the law you yourself made.
Judge fairly and keep your good reputation.
Tell a true friend from a flatterer: a friend is consistent and speaks frankly, while a flatterer imitates and praises.
When correcting a friend, speak frankly but tactfully and privately, mixing praise with criticism.
Control anger by delaying action, keeping silent, and noting how ugly angry people look.
entries.argued_against: giving way to rage, punishing in anger

entries.advice: Avoid talkativeness: keep secrets and answer only what is asked.
Stop prying into others' troubles; turn curiosity to nature or your own faults.
Benefit from enemies, who watch you closely; live carefully and bear their insults calmly.
Find tranquility by comparing yourself with those worse off and enjoying what you have.
Keep healthy with moderate eating, exercise like reading aloud, and avoiding overindulgence.
In marriage, share friends, property, and gods, and treat one another gently.
Educate children with care: mothers nurse them, choose good tutors, and use praise rather than beatings.
Listen quietly to lectures, attend to content not style, and ask relevant questions.
Read poetry critically, drawing moral lessons and remembering that poets often say false things.
Avoid superstition, which fears the gods as tyrants; it is worse than disbelief.
Grieve moderately for the dead and avoid excessive mourning.
Love your siblings, share inheritance generously, and settle quarrels quickly.
Have a few good friends rather than many.
Praise yourself only when necessary, such as in self-defense or to encourage others.
Overcome false shame by learning to refuse improper requests, practicing first in small matters.
Old men should keep serving the public.
entries.argued_against: those who say old men should retire

entries.advice: Enter public life from conviction rather than ambition, govern mildly, and settle civic disputes.
Rulers should take philosophers as advisers.
Measure moral progress by caring less about reputation and acting on what you learn.
Consider whether eating meat is necessary, given its cruelty to animals.
Seek rest in the deity, since the human heart stays restless until it does.
Confess your sins openly to the deity, to praise it and to help others turn back.
Rely on divine grace rather than your own will, which can't overcome sin alone.
Don't delay conversion by saying 'not yet'; break bad habits now.
Beware how habit hardens into a chain that binds the will.
Beware sinful companionship: wrongdoing grows when done for friends' approval.
Love people in the deity, not as if they were permanent, to avoid crushing grief.
Avoid theatrical shows that make you enjoy pity and passion for fiction.
Avoid gladiatorial shows, which inflame cruelty.
Reject astrology and fortune telling, which shift blame for sin onto the stars.
Reject the dualist sect's teaching that evil is a substance; evil is lack of good.
Read scripture humbly instead of despising its simple style.
Value truth over eloquence, judging teachers by content not style.
Love wisdom above wealth and fame.
Eat and drink as medicine, for need rather than pleasure.
Guard against idle curiosity, even watching trivial things like a dog chasing a hare.
Guard against love of praise and the wish to be feared or loved for your own sake.
In church singing, attend more to the words than to the melody.
Look within yourself, through memory, to find the deity.
Pursue chastity and freedom from lust.
Learn and teach for truth, not for worldly success, and don't beat schoolboys for trivial failures.
Aim at happiness: a complete life of rational activity in line with virtue.
entries.argued_against: those identifying happiness with pleasure, honor, or wealth

entries.advice: Seek the mean between excess and deficiency, relative to you.
Build virtue by habit, doing just and brave acts repeatedly.
entries.argued_against: those who think theory alone makes people good

entries.advice: To hit the mean, avoid the worse extreme and lean toward the side opposite your tendency.
Be especially wary of pleasure, which biases judgment.
Face fearful things bravely for noble reasons, especially death in battle.
Be moderate in bodily pleasures like food, drink, and sex.
Give money to the right people, in the right amount, at the right time.
Claim the honor you deserve, being neither vain nor falsely humble.
Be angry at the right things, with the right people, to the right degree.
Be truthful about yourself, witty but not buffoonish, and friendly in social life.
Be just: distribute by merit and correct unfair gains and losses.
Use equity to correct the law when its generality fails.
Develop practical wisdom to deliberate well about what to do.
Avoid weakness of will, acting against your better judgment.
Value friendships based on virtue above those for pleasure or use.
Keep only a few close friends.
Engage in contemplation as the highest happiness, insofar as you can.
Support good laws and upbringing to train citizens in virtue.
Don't expect more precision than the subject allows.
The young and passion-driven should not study ethics or politics.
Love the best, rational part of yourself, not wealth or pleasure.
Have enough external goods, like health, wealth, and friends, to live well.
Choose actions deliberately and own the responsibility.
Don't trust Fortune; she is changeable by nature.
entries.argued_against: those who expect Fortune to be steady

entries.advice: Count the blessings you still have, such as family.
Recognize wealth, office, power, fame, and pleasure as false goods that can't make you happy.
Seek true happiness in the deity, the highest good.
Despise fame, as the earth is a speck in the cosmos.
Trust that the wicked are powerless and punished while good people are rewarded by virtue.
entries.argued_against: those who think the wicked flourish

entries.advice: Pity the wicked rather than hating them; they are sick.
Accept that providence orders all things; all fortune is good.
entries.argued_against: those who see events as chance

entries.advice: Keep hoping and praying, as free will remains alongside divine foreknowledge.
Reject poetry that nourishes grief.
Look up toward heaven, as humans stand upright to do.
Remember you are a rational being; forgetting your nature causes misery.
Value adversity, which teaches and reveals true friends.
Pray for divine help before seeking the highest good.
Don't think office makes you worthy; honor comes from virtue.
Don't prize bodily beauty or strength, which are fleeting.
Do good, knowing the deity sees all.
Be just, since justice is better for its own sake and its consequences.
entries.argued_against: the view that justice is the advantage of the stronger or a mere convention

entries.advice: Order your soul so that reason rules, spirit supports it, and appetite obeys.
Pursue philosophy and knowledge of the good above all.
Let philosophers rule, since only they know the good.
entries.argued_against: rule by the ignorant or by the ambitious

entries.advice: Rulers should not own private property or wealth, so they are not corrupted.
Censor poetry that portrays the deities as wicked or heroes as cowardly.
Each person should do the one job suited to their nature.
Educate the young through balanced music and gymnastics to temper the soul.
Women with suitable natures should receive the same education and roles as men among the guardians.
entries.argued_against: the view that sex disqualifies from ruling

entries.advice: Turn the soul from shadows toward the real, and return to help others.
Avoid tyranny of the passions; the tyrant is the most miserable of men.
Value the pleasures of reason above those of honor or appetite.
Avoid imitative poetry that strengthens the irrational parts of the soul.
Live justly because souls face judgment and reincarnation after death.
Avoid both excessive wealth and poverty in the city, as both corrupt.
Guardians should share families, wives, and children in common.
Do not give back to someone what is owed if it harms them, like weapons to a madman.
Do not harm anyone, even enemies; harming makes people worse.
Postpone dialectic until maturity to avoid lawless questioning by the young.
Rulers may use noble lies for the good of the city.
Never pursue advantage at the cost of what is morally right; true expediency never conflicts with honor.
entries.argued_against: those who separate the useful from the right

entries.advice: Practice the four virtues: wisdom, justice, courage, and moderation.
Harm no one unless wronged, and respect common and private property.
Keep promises and good faith, even with enemies.
Give generously but within your means, to the deserving, without harming others.
Rank duties: country and parents first, then children and family, then friends.
Make war only to secure peace, after formal demands, and spare those who surrender.
Hold externals in contempt and value civic courage above military glory.
entries.argued_against: those prizing military over civil achievement

entries.advice: If capable, serve in public life rather than withdrawing.
